title: Disentangling Generation and Regression in Stochastic Interpolants for ControllableImage Restoration

paper.title: Disentangling Generation and Regression in Stochastic Interpolants for Controllable Image Restoration
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent advances in Image Restoration (IR) have been largely driven by generative methods such as Diffusion Models and Flow Matching, which excel in synthesizing realistic textures while suffering from slow multi-step inference and compromised pixel fidelity.
In contrast, classical regression-based IR methods excel precisely in these aspects, offering single-step efficiency and high pixel-level reconstruction fidelity.
To bridge this gap, we propose DiSI , a unified framework that Di sentangles the underlying S tochastic I nterpolant process into independent generation and regression components.
This decoupling endows DiSI with remarkable versatility, enabling a continuous and controllable transition from a pure regression process to a fully generative one.
Technically, we instantiate this framework with two specific sampling trajectories, accompanied by a unified sampler for high-quality, few-step inference on arbitrary trajectories.
Furthermore, we design a dual-branch U-Net style transformer network in pixel space, using a dedicated branch to enhance conditional guidance while ensuring high throughput.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiSI efficiently achieves competitive results on various IR tasks, while uniquely offering the inference-time flexibility to control the distortion-perception trade-off within a single model.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Image Restoration (IR) is a fundamental and long-standing problem in low-level vision that involves restoring high-quality images from their low-quality ( i.e . , degraded) counterparts [ 91 ] . It encompasses multiple tasks, including image super-resolution [ 38 , 81 , 65 , 103 , 102 ] , denoising [ 98 , 14 , 9 ] , and inpainting [ 58 , 39 , 50 ] . Solving these problems is essential for enhancing image quality and usability. Advances in deep learning have inspired a paradigm of regression-based IR methods, where networks [ 41 , 97 ] are trained to map degraded images to clean ones by minimizing a pixel-wise loss ( e.g . , MSE) [ 74 ] . Despite their efficiency and high performance on various distortion metrics ( e.g . , PSNR), they often yield over-smoothed or unrealistic textures, compromising perceptual quality [ 3 ] . To synthesize realistic textures, IR has embraced generative models, with Diffusion Models (DMs) [ 25 , 71 , 72 ] and Flow Matching (FM) [ 46 , 42 ] now dominating this field. DMs and FMs involve a forward process adding noise, and a backward process reconstructing samples from Gaussian noise (see Fig. 1 a), conditioned on degraded images [ 11 , 65 ] . However, this is unnecessary and inefficient for IR, as the degraded image itself offers a better starting point than pure noise. This insight inspires recent works, e.g . , residual diffusion models [ 94 , 45 ] , Mean-Reverting Diffusion Models (MRDMs) [ 52 , 53 ] , and Diffusion Bridges (DBs) [ 106 , 44 , 93 ] , to construct a direct degraded-to-clean diffusion path. A unifying framework is provided by Stochastic Interpolants (SIs) [ 1 , 55 ] that generalize DMs/FMs by defining transitions between arbitrary distributions. This naturally supports direct degraded-to-clean paths (see Fig. 1 b), particularly suitable for IR [ 2 ] . Despite their powerful ability to synthesize realistic textures, DM/FM-based generative IR methods introduce a critical trade-off. They require expensive multi-step inference and often sacrifice the pixel-level fidelity in exchange for their remarkable perceptual quality [ 52 , 44 , 2 ] . In contrast, high-fidelity restoration and single-step efficiency are precisely where the regression paradigm [ 97 , 41 ] excels. This fundamental dichotomy between distortion and perception [ 3 ] , separating regressive methods that prioritize fidelity and efficiency from generative methods that achieve perceptual quality at a high cost, motivates the following question: Can we develop a unified framework to seamlessly bridge regression and generation, thereby enabling fine-grained control over both aspects? To answer this question, this paper presents DiSI , a new framework that Di sentangles generation and regression within S tochastic I nterpolants ( Fig. 1 c). In standard SIs ( Fig. 1 b) [ 2 , 1 ] , the generative capability stems from the stochastic noise term γ t ​ 𝒛 \gamma_{t}\bm{z} , while the deterministic path between 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} and 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} inherently constitutes a regression. DiSI decouples these by introducing two independent time variables: Regression Time r r governing the deterministic transition, and Generation Time g g controlling noise injection. This explicit separation directly bridges regression and generation, enabling fine-grained control over the fundamental distortion-perception trade-off. As shown in Fig. 1 d, DiSI can seamlessly transition from a one-step, high-fidelity regression that over-smooths textures, to a multi-step generation process capable of synthesizing rich, realistic details. In the DiSI framework, we design two specific sampling trajectories: an elliptical trajectory analogous to DBs [ 44 , 106 , 93 ] and a linear trajectory inspired by MRDMs [ 52 , 53 ] . We also introduce a unified efficient first-order sampler, enabling high-quality, few-step restoration on arbitrary trajectories. To further improve performance and efficiency, we propose a novel dual-branch U-Net style transformer (DULiT) in pixel space, inspired by [ 17 , 88 , 97 ] . It strengthens conditional guidance from degraded images via its dual-branch design, while incorporating efficient modules like linear attention [ 33 ] to ensure high throughput. Our technical contributions are: 1) DiSI, a novel framework that decouples regression and generation within SI for controllable distortion-perception balance. 2) Two sampling trajectories accompanied by an efficient and analytically derived sampler for fast, high-quality inference. 3) A dual-branch pixel-space network that strengthens conditional guidance while maintaining high efficiency.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Image Restoration. IR is a long-standing and fundamental problem in low-level vision, with tasks such as image deraining [ 90 ] , deblurring [ 100 ] , and super-resolution [ 82 ] . Deep learning has established neural networks as the prevailing IR approach, commonly implemented via convolutional architectures [ 103 , 102 , 4 , 98 ] or vision transformers [ 97 , 60 , 41 , 6 ] , and trained with regression losses. While these methods achieve strong distortion metrics like PSNR and SSIM [ 83 ] , they often yield unrealistic outputs in highly ill-posed scenarios like inpainting [ 87 , 50 ] . The advancement of IR has been significantly driven by generative models [ 22 , 25 ] , with DMs and FMs now dominating the field [ 40 , 23 ] . Most DM/FM-based IR methods start from pure noise and condition on degraded images [ 50 , 86 , 80 , 64 , 65 , 10 ] . Others, more aligned with our work, modify the initial distribution to incorporate degraded inputs, including MRDMs [ 52 , 53 ] , Diffusion Bridges (DBs) [ 93 , 44 , 106 , 104 ] , and SI models [ 2 ] . While generative IR methods excel at producing realistic textures, they may compromise pixel-level fidelity. Diffusion Models. DMs [ 12 ] are a prominent class of probabilistic generative models [ 76 ] for image synthesis [ 16 ] , pioneered by DDPM [ 25 ] and NCSN [ 71 ] . Since their introduction, the theoretical scope of DMs has been significantly extended by Score Matching [ 72 , 31 ] and, more recently Flow Matching (FM) [ 42 , 46 ] with the concept of differential equations. The latter have already become foundational to image generation [ 17 , 62 ] . A broader perspective is offered by Stochastic Interpolant (SI) [ 1 , 55 ] , a generalized framework bridging arbitrary distributions that unifies DMs and FMs, providing our theoretical basis. The rapid evolution of DMs and FMs has catalyzed significant advancements, with innovations in network architecture and sampling efficiency being particularly relevant to this work. Architecturally, backbones have transitioned from standard U-Nets [ 57 , 16 ] to scalable Transformers [ 79 ] ( e.g . , DiT [ 59 ] and MM-DiT [ 17 ] ), with recent research increasingly prioritizing efficiency [ 88 , 13 , 7 ] . Concurrently, substantial efforts have focused on accelerating the iterative inference process [ 18 , 70 , 46 , 21 , 48 , 47 ] , where advanced solvers like DDIM [ 69 ] and DPM-Solver [ 48 , 49 , 105 ] reduce sampling steps while maintaining generation quality.

sections.heading: 3.2 DiSI: A Unified Framework
sections.text: Our work is based on a key observation: the generative power of DMs, FMs, and SIs [ 72 , 43 , 1 ] stems from stochastic noise injection ( i.e . , 𝒛 \bm{z} in Fig. 1 ). We adopt the SI framework because it unifies these models and fits IR’s data-to-data nature [ 2 ] . However, standard SIs have a critical limitation: they fuse the deterministic regression path with the stochastic generative process by coupling both to a single time variable t t . Hence, our core insight is that fine-grained control over the regression-generation balance requires disentangling these processes. Motivated by this insight, we reformulate the standard SI process in Eq. 1 by introducing two independent time variables ( Fig. 1 c): 1) a Regression Time r r governing the data-to-data transition ( i.e . , 𝒙 1 → 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{1}\to\bm{x}_{0} ), and 2) a Generation Time g g controlling the injected noise 𝒛 \bm{z} . This decoupling yields our DiSI process: 𝒙 ⁡ ( r , g ) = λ g ​ ( α r ​ 𝒙 0 + β r ​ 𝒙 1 ) + γ g ​ 𝒛 , \bm{x}(r,g)=\lambda_{g}(\alpha_{r}\bm{x}_{0}+\beta_{r}\bm{x}_{1})+\gamma_{g}\bm{z}, (3) where ( α r , β r ) (\alpha_{r},\beta_{r}) and ( λ g , γ g ) (\lambda_{g},\gamma_{g}) are the regression and generation coefficients, governed by r r and g g , respectively. This formulation explicitly disentangles the regression path α r ​ 𝒙 0 + β r ​ 𝒙 1 \alpha_{r}\bm{x}_{0}+\beta_{r}\bm{x}_{1} from the noise injection, overcoming the single-variable constraint of standard SIs and enabling independent control of the two processes. Analogous to standard DMs, FMs, and SIs, the marginal distribution of 𝒙 ⁡ ( r , g ) \bm{x}(r,g) evolves according to a PF-ODE [ 66 ] . DiSI generalizes this via two time variables, yielding an exact differential equation with two distinct vector fields: d ​ 𝒙 ​ ( r , g ) = 𝒗 r θ ​ d ​ r + 𝒗 g θ ​ d ​ g , \mathrm{d}\bm{x}\left(r,g\right)=\bm{v}_{r}^{\theta}\mathrm{d}r+\bm{v}_{g}^{\theta}\mathrm{d}g, (4) where 𝒗 r θ \bm{v}_{r}^{\theta} and 𝒗 g θ \bm{v}_{g}^{\theta} are the velocities along the r r and g g axes ( Fig. 1 c). We train a network ℱ θ \mathcal{F}_{\theta} , parameterized by θ \theta , to estimate these velocities, as detailed later. Coefficient Schedule. The coefficient schedule, which defines the formulation of coefficients in Eq. 3 , significantly affects performance. While early methods often adopt designs like linear schedules [ 46 , 42 ] , recent works [ 55 , 47 ] highlight the benefits of variance-preserving (VP) schedules, which stabilize training by maintaining constant input variance [ 31 , 27 ] . Adhering to this principle, following [ 55 ] , we design our coefficients as a generalized VP (GVP) formulation: α r = 1 2 ​ ( cos ⁡ r 1 + ρ − sin ⁡ r 1 − ρ ) , β r = 1 2 ​ ( cos ⁡ r 1 + ρ + sin ⁡ r 1 − ρ ) λ g = cos ⁡ g , γ g = sin ⁡ g , \begin{aligned} \alpha_{r}&=\cfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\frac{\cos{r}}{\sqrt{1+\rho}}-\frac{\sin{r}}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right),&\beta_{r}&=\cfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\frac{\cos{r}}{\sqrt{1+\rho}}+\frac{\sin{r}}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)\\ \lambda_{g}&=\cos g,&\gamma_{g}&=\sin g\end{aligned}, (5) where the definitions of α r \alpha_{r} and β r \beta_{r} incorporate ρ \rho , the correlation coefficient between 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} and 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} . This design is crucial for IR where clean and degraded images are inherently correlated ( ρ ≠ 0 \rho\neq 0 ). The inclusion of ρ \rho ensures that Eq. 5 satisfies the GVP property (see Sec. 0.A.1 ). We select the minimal ranges r ∈ [ − φ , φ ] r\in[-\varphi,\varphi] and g ∈ [ 0 , π 2 ] g\in[0,\frac{\pi}{2}] that span the full coefficient evolution, where φ = arcsin ⁡ 1 − ρ 2 \varphi=\arcsin{\sqrt{\frac{1-\rho}{2}}} , yielding the boundaries 𝒙 ⁡ ( − φ , 0 ) = 𝒙 0 \bm{x}(-\varphi,0)=\bm{x}_{0} , 𝒙 ⁡ ( φ , 0 ) = 𝒙 1 \bm{x}(\varphi,0)=\bm{x}_{1} and 𝒙 ⁡ ( ⋅ , π 2 ) = 𝒛 \bm{x}(\cdot,\frac{\pi}{2})=\bm{z} . Network Parameterization. The parameterization of the network’s prediction goal is a key design in DMs. While previous approaches predict the noise 𝒛 \bm{z} [ 25 , 57 , 16 ] , target 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} [ 31 , 32 ] , score ∇ 𝒙 ​ log ​ p t ​ ( 𝒙 ) \nabla_{\bm{x}}\log p_{t}(\bm{x}) [ 72 , 71 , 106 ] , or velocity 𝒗 t \bm{v}_{t} [ 42 , 46 , 43 ] , these goals are known to be theoretically interchangeable within the SI framework [ 1 , 55 ] . But the choice can significantly impact empirical performance. In DiSI, the 𝒗 r , 𝒗 g ↔ 𝒙 0 \bm{v}_{r},\bm{v}_{g}\leftrightarrow\bm{x}_{0} conversion is mathematically inherent under any schedule, as 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} is the only intrinsic unknown. Thus, we choose to predict 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} , since jointly predicting ( 𝒗 r , 𝒗 g ) (\bm{v}_{r},\bm{v}_{g}) forces the network to implicitly satisfy their geometric consistency, degrading performance (see Tab. 7 ). sections.heading: 3.4 Inference
sections.text: While training decouples r r and g g , inference demands an explicit path ( r ⁡ ( t ) , g ⁡ ( t ) ) (r(t),g(t)) bridging degraded and clean distributions. Although DiSI supports any path satisfying 𝒙 ⁡ ( − φ , 0 ) = 𝒙 0 \bm{x}(-\varphi,0)=\bm{x}_{0} , we prioritize geometric smoothness for stable ODE integration and generation, as validated in Tab. 6 . Thus, we propose two specific choices: Elliptical and Linear ( Fig. 2 ), as the simplest smooth curves to model the behaviors of DBs [ 106 ] and MRDMs [ 52 ] , respectively. Finally, we introduce a universal, analytically derived ODE-based sampler for any trajectory. Elliptical Trajectory. To model DBs [ 44 , 106 , 93 ] connecting noiseless 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} and 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} with pure intermediate noise, we employ an elliptical path ( Fig. 2 (a)): r = φ ​ sin ⁡ t , g = δ ​ cos ⁡ t t ∈ [ − π 2 , π 2 ] , r=\varphi\sin{t},g=\delta\cos{t}\qquad t\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right], (9) which satisfies the elliptical equation r 2 φ 2 + g 2 δ 2 = 1 \frac{r^{2}}{\varphi^{2}}+\frac{g^{2}}{\delta^{2}}=1 , with hyperparameter δ ∈ [ 0 , π 2 ] \delta\in[0,\frac{\pi}{2}] controlling the peak noise level. A key property of our DiSI framework is that all inference trajectories stem from the same underlying PF-ODE in Eq. 4 . This allows us to develop a sampler that is not specific to any particular path. While basic numerical ( e.g . , Euler’s) solvers [ 31 ] require many steps to minimize discretization errors, we derive a specific few-step solver for DiSI. Inspired by DPM-Solver [ 48 , 105 , 49 ] , our sampler analytically solves the linear portion of the PF-ODE in Eq. 4 and linearly approximates the isolated non-linear term (see Sec. 0.A.3 ), supporting much larger step sizes and enabling high-quality generation in very few steps. sections.heading: 3.5 Efficient Network
sections.text: Our network ℱ θ \mathcal{F}_{\theta} integrates a hierarchical D ual-branch U -Net style backbone with efficient Li near T ransformer blocks, termed DULiT (see Fig. 3 ). It operates in pixel space, unlike the prevailing latent-space paradigm [ 62 ] , to avoid the information loss of compression and preserve fine textures crucial for IR [ 92 ] . Figure 3 : DULiT architecture. Left : Backbone (feature resolutions at bottom). Right : Modules including (a) Two-Time Encoder and (b) DULiT Block, which comprises the (c) Linear Attention Module, (d) JLA layer, and (e) FFN. Dimensions b , n , c b,n,c denote batch size, sequence length, and channels. Modules in dashed borders are optional. A. DULiT Backbone. We adopt a dual-branch structure from MM-DiT [ 17 ] to enhance conditional guidance, processing the noisy state 𝒙 ⁡ ( r , g ) \bm{x}\left(r,g\right) and the degraded image 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} in parallel. However, the constant-resolution pipeline of DiT backbones [ 59 , 17 ] is computationally expensive. To address this, we integrate the dual-branch design into a hierarchical U-Net backbone, motivated by [ 63 , 13 , 97 ] . As shown in Fig. 3 , the DULiT backbone features a three-stage encoder with L 1 L_{1} , L 2 L_{2} , L 3 L_{3} DULiT blocks, a middle layer with L 4 L_{4} blocks, and a symmetric decoder. The encoder downsamples features via PixelUnshuffle [ 68 ] and 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution, while the decoder upsamples using 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution and PixelShuffle [ 68 ] . Dual-Branch Skip Connections are applied per branch at each resolution level. Inspired by HDiT [ 13 ] , we use an efficient learnable linear interpolation (lerp) for image fusions. Input and output features are processed with 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolutions, augmented by a long-range residual connection that improves performance. To accelerate convergence, following [ 31 , 32 ] , we zero-initialize all DULiT output projections and replace biases with a channel of ones concatenated to the input. B. DULiT Block. The core computational unit for all stages is our DULiT Block (see Fig. 3 (b)). We use AdaGroupNorm [ 16 ] for time conditioning, which, unlike AdaLayerNorm used in DiT [ 59 ] , avoids costly reshape operations. Within each block, the Joint Linear Attention (JLA) layer is the only cross-branch interaction module, followed by FeedForward Networks (FFNs) for both branches. C. JLA Layer. The Joint Linear Attention (JLA) layer forms the core of our DULiT Block. To address the prohibitive quadratic complexity of vanilla attention [ 79 , 59 ] in high-resolution pixel space, following Sana [ 88 ] , we employ ReLU linear attention [ 33 ] ( Fig. 3 (c)) that eliminates the softmax operator and reorders matrix operations for linear computational complexity. Our key innovation lies in its joint design ( Fig. 3 (d)): features from both noisy and conditional branches pass through efficient Projection blocks, which are composed of 1 × 1 1\times 1 Conv and 3 × 3 3\times 3 DWConv layers inspired by [ 26 , 97 ] , to generate dual-branch 𝑸 \bm{Q} , 𝑲 \bm{K} , and 𝑽 \bm{V} . These tensors are concatenated along the sequence dimension, a strategy empirically superior to channel-wise fusion as validated in Tab. 7 . To ensure efficiency, we accelerate the entire JLA layer using torch.compile . D. FFN. The DULiT Block concludes with an efficient FFN ( Fig. 3 (e)). It replaces the FFN in MM-DiT [ 17 ] with a computationally efficient design, using the same Projection block as in the JLA layer, and a GELU activation. E. Time Embedding and Modulation. Time variables ( r , g ) (r,g) are individually encoded and summed into a token t t ( Fig. 3 (a)). As in DiT [ 59 ] , t t is projected per block to generate scale/shift parameters for both branches, modulating normalized features before JLA and FFN ( Fig. 3 (b)). Notably, our experiments in Tab. 7 show that the post-modulation steps ( ξ ⋅ 1 \xi_{\cdot}^{1} , ξ ⋅ 2 \xi_{\cdot}^{2} ) are unnecessary in DULiT. F. Positional Embeddings. Following Sana [ 88 ] , we omit positional embeddings ( e.g . , RoPE [ 73 ] ), since convolutions inherently capture positions [ 28 ] .

sections.heading: 4.1 Comparative Experiments
sections.text: We compare DiSI against SOTA IR approaches, the results are in Tabs. 4 , 4 , 4 and 4 and visual comparisons are in Figs. 4 , 6 , 7 and 7 . Best and second-best results are highlighted and underlined , with ↑ \uparrow / ↓ \downarrow indicating higher/lower is better performance. DM/FM-based methods are marked in gray . We report DiSI using the proposed elliptical sampler in Algorithm 1 and its corresponding elliptical path. Results with other training schemes and trajectories are in Appendix 0.F . To demonstrate flexible trade-offs between regression and generation, we present two variants: (1) DiSI-R for fidelity via noiseless ( δ = 0 \delta=0 , i.e . , regression) sampling, and (2) DiSI-G for perceptual quality via noisy ( δ > 0 \delta>0 ) sampling. Both share the same trained weights and only differ in sampling parameters (see Sec. 0.D.1 ). Based on the results, we observe: (1) DM/FM-based baselines excel in perceptual metrics ( e.g . , LPIPS, FID) but lag in distortion metrics ( e.g . , PSNR, SSIM), and their multi-step inference incurs significant computational overhead. (2) DiSI generally achieves competitive or even SOTA performance across the four tasks, demonstrating strong restoration capability. (3) DiSI-R excels in distortion metrics with high efficiency, while DiSI-G achieves remarkable perceptual quality at increased computational cost. Visually, DiSI-R often yields over-smoothed results, whereas DiSI-G produces realistic textures (see Fig. 7 ). Crucially, this transition requires no retraining and is achieved solely by tuning sampling parameters ( e.g . , δ \delta and sampling steps), enabling a controllable distortion-perception performance balance within a single trained model. (4) DiSI outperforms DM/FM-based baselines in efficiency while maintaining competitive generative performance, owing to our DULiT network and few-step sampler.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce DiSI, a unified SI-based framework for controllable IR that decouples regression and generation, enabling a single model to flexibly balance distortion and perception. Our implementation integrates two sampling trajectories, an analytically derived sampler for fast, high-quality inference, and a dual-branch pixel-space network that strengthens conditional guidance with high efficiency. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness and efficiency of DiSI for IR.

sections.heading: Appendix 0.B Connection between DiSI and Stochastic Interpolants
sections.text: Fundamentally, DiSI serves as a generalized extension of the standard SI framework [ 1 ] . As discussed in Sec. 3.2 , DiSI differs from standard SIs by decoupling the single time variable into regression time r r and generation time g g . This decoupling enables independent control over the transition between 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} and 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} and the generative process governed by noise injection of 𝒛 \bm{z} . Once an explicit functional relationship between r r and g g is specified, DiSI reduces to a conventional one-dimensional SI process. The Elliptical and Linear trajectories exemplify this reduction. Below, we analyze the connection between DiSI and SIs under these trajectories and discuss the Regression Trajectory as a special case in detail.

sections.heading: Appendix 0.C Algorithms
sections.text: This section presents pseudo-code for training ( Sec. 3.3 ) and inference ( Sec. 3.4 ).

sections.heading: 0.C.1 Training Algorithm
sections.text: Algorithm 3 summarizes the training procedure of DiSI. As described in Sec. 3.3 , training takes as input a clean image 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} , its degraded counterpart 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} , the denoising network ℱ θ \mathcal{F}_{\theta} , and the adaptive weighting MLP w ϕ w_{\phi} . In each iteration, we first draw a pair of time variables ( r , g ) (r,g) using the chosen Time Sampler (Generalist or Specialist). We then draw noise 𝒛 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ d 2 ​ 𝑰 ) \bm{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{d}^{2}\bm{I}) and construct the noisy intermediate state 𝒙 ⁡ ( r , g ) \bm{x}(r,g) according to the DiSI process in Eq. 3 . At the same time, following EDM2 [ 32 ] , the adaptive loss weight w w is produced by an MLP w ϕ w_{\phi} conditioned on ( r , g ) (r,g) , with ϕ \phi as its parameters. The network ℱ θ \mathcal{F}_{\theta} then takes the normalized noisy state 𝒙 ⁡ ( r , g ) σ d \frac{\bm{x}(r,g)}{\sigma_{d}} , the degraded image 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} , and the joint time embeddings of ( r , g ) (r,g) as input to predict the clean image 𝒙 ^ 0 \hat{\bm{x}}_{0} (see Eq. 7 ). Finally, the model parameters θ \theta and the weighting parameters ϕ \phi are jointly updated using the objective in Eq. 8 . This procedure is repeated until convergence.

sections.heading: Inference Algorithm for Generation Trajectory.
sections.text: Algorithm 4 summarizes DiSI inference for the Elliptical and Linear trajectories using the hybrid sampler in Eq. 11 . The time variable t t is discretized into N N steps along the chosen trajectory, from π 2 \frac{\pi}{2} to − π 2 -\frac{\pi}{2} for the Elliptical path and from 1 1 to 0 0 for the Linear path. The initial state 𝒙 r N , g N \bm{x}_{r_{N},g_{N}} is then constructed from the degraded image 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} and sampled noise 𝒛 \bm{z} according to the corresponding trajectory definition. At each denoising step i i , the network ℱ θ \mathcal{F}_{\theta} predicts the clean image 𝒙 ^ 0 \hat{\bm{x}}_{0} based on the current state 𝒙 r i , g i \bm{x}_{r_{i},g_{i}} , the degraded image 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} , and the joint time embedding ( r i , g i ) (r_{i},g_{i}) . For the Elliptical trajectory, the first step ( i = N i=N ) uses a fully stochastic update ( η = 1 \eta=1 ) to avoid the singularity at g = 0 g=0 , as mentioned in Sec. 3.4 . All remaining steps, as well as the entire Linear trajectory, use the standard hybrid sampler, where η \eta controls the injected stochasticity via the noise coefficient κ \kappa . sections.heading: Inference Algorithm for Regression Trajectory.
sections.text: Algorithm 5 describes the inference procedure for the regression path ( δ = 0 \delta=0 in both the Elliptical and Linear cases). Unlike the general sampler, the generation time is explicitly fixed at g = 0 g=0 , while the regression time r r is discretized from φ \varphi to − φ -\varphi . Accordingly, the initial state 𝒙 r N , g N \bm{x}_{r_{N},g_{N}} is set to the degraded image 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} without noise injection. At each denoising step, the network predicts the clean image 𝒙 ^ 0 \hat{\bm{x}}_{0} . Since g g is fixed at 0 0 , the update rule simplifies to the deterministic form derived in Eq. 13 . This yields a multi-step regression process that progressively refines 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} toward 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} . When N = 1 N=1 , the sampler reduces to standard one-step regression.

sections.heading: Correlation Coefficient.
sections.text: We compute ρ \rho as the average correlation coefficient across all degraded-clean pairs in the training set, and apply it during testing.

sections.heading: Model Complexity.
sections.text: The computational complexity and parameter count remain consistent across all tasks due to the same architecture. We report a computational cost of 128.67 GMACs (Giga-Multiply-ACcumulate operations) and 32.49M parameters, measured via ptflops with a 1 × 3 × 256 × 256 1\times 3\times 256\times 256 input.

sections.heading: Training Protocol.
sections.text: For a fair comparison, following IR-SDE [ 52 ] , we train all models for 500k steps with a global batch size of 16 (4 per GPU). To handle varying image resolutions, we retain the IR-SDE cropping strategy, but leverage the inherent efficiency of our model to enlarge the training patch size from 128 × 128 128\times 128 to 256 × 256 256\times 256 . Finally, we use the Elliptical Specialist Time Sampler om Algorithm 1 for training. Since our inference variants, DiSI-R and DiSI-G, are both based on the Elliptical path (with the former being a special case), this strategy ensures the model is optimized for the corresponding sampling path.

sections.heading: Network Configuration.
sections.text: The network architecture is fixed across all tasks, adopting the optimal configuration from our ablation studies in Sec. 4.2 . Specifically, we omit positional embeddings and post-modulation scales ( ξ ⋅ ⋅ \xi_{\cdot}^{\cdot} ), retaining only pre-modulation shifts ( ε ⋅ ⋅ \varepsilon_{\cdot}^{\cdot} ) and scales ( ζ ⋅ ⋅ \zeta_{\cdot}^{\cdot} ). We also use adaptive loss weighting and Conv projections ( 1 × 1 1\times 1 Conv + 3 × 3 3\times 3 DWConv) for JLA and FFN.

sections.heading: Optimization.
sections.text: We train the model with AdamW at a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} . We further apply EMA with a decay rate of 0.9999 to stabilize training.

sections.heading: Inference Configuration.
sections.text: We employ two inference variants, DiSI-R and DiSI-G, sharing identical model weights. (1) DiSI-R maximizes efficiency and fidelity. It uses a single-step Regression Trajectory ( δ = 0 , N = 1 \delta=0,N=1 ), functioning as a deterministic end-to-end regression model. (2) DiSI-G targets high perceptual quality with moderate efficiency. We use the Elliptical path with N = 10 N=10 since it introduces generative capability without the severe fidelity degradation of the Linear path (see Tab. 8 ). To resolve DiSI-G’s initial singularity, we apply a stochastic booting step ( η = 1 \eta=1 , ϵ = 10 − 3 \epsilon=10^{-3} ), with η = 0 \eta=0 for subsequent steps.

sections.heading: Image Deraining.
sections.text: We categorize the metrics in Tab. 4 into two types: (1) Performance Metrics ( e.g . , PSNR, SSIM): Most baseline scores are adopted directly from GOUB [ 93 ] , except for FoD [ 51 ] , which is sourced from its original paper. (2) Efficiency Metrics (Params, Lat.): To ensure a consistent benchmark, we re-evaluate these across all methods using their official codebases. A notable exception for latency is the JAX-based MAXIM [ 77 ] , which we optimize with jax.compile to accurately reflect its full efficiency.

sections.heading: Image Deblurring.
sections.text: For the deblurring comparison results in Tab. 4 , we adopt performance metrics for most baselines directly from IR-SDE [ 52 ] . We re-evaluate efficiency metrics for all methods to ensure consistency, including the jax.compile optimization for MAXIM [ 77 ] . Notably, for DeepDeblur [ 56 ] , all the metrics reported derive from a modern pytorch reimplementation, since this version yields slight performance gains over the original lua codebase.

sections.heading: Low-Light Enhancement.
sections.text: Most performance metrics in Tab. 4 are sourced from DA-CLIP [ 54 ] . However, we exclude DA-CLIP, as its all-in-one paradigm is incompatible with our task-specific setup. For other baselines, we report FoD [ 51 ] metrics from its original paper and re-train GOUB [ 93 ] . Efficiency metrics are re-evaluated as above, retaining the jax.compile optimization for MAXIM [ 77 ] .

sections.heading: Image Inpainting.
sections.text: Metrics for PromptIR [ 78 ] , DDRM [ 34 ] , and IR-SDE [ 52 ] are adopted from the IR-SDE paper. Moreover, we re-train GOUB [ 93 ] and FoD [ 51 ] for inpainting to report the remaining results in Tab. 4 . As in previous tasks, we evaluate efficiency across all methods using their official implementations.

sections.heading: 0.D.3 Implementation Details for Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We adhere to the evaluation protocol of IR-SDE [ 52 ] for all metric calculations. • Distortion Metrics (PSNR, SSIM): We rescale and clamp pixel values to [ 0,255 ] [0,255] . Computations are performed on RGB channels, with the exception of image deraining, which utilizes the Y channel (YCbCr space). • Perception Metrics: We compute LPIPS [ 101 ] using its official implementation with the AlexNet [ 35 ] backbone, scaling inputs to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . FID [ 24 ] is calculated via pytorch-fid with InceptionV3 [ 75 ] backbone, comparing the restored images against the ground truth of the test set. • Efficiency Metrics: We compute parameter counts using the ptflops library. For latency, we ensure precise GPU timing via torch.cuda.Event and torch.cuda.synchronize , reporting the average across the test set.

sections.heading: 0.D.4 Implementation Details for Ablation Studies
sections.text: This section outlines the setup of ablation studies in Secs. 4.2 and 0.F.1 .

sections.heading: Ablation on Optimization Settings.
sections.text: Our deraining ablation baseline adopts the default configurations in Tab. 10 under DiSI-R sampling, except we disable adaptive loss weighting and use Linear FFN projections. Using this baseline, we investigate the impact of the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) decay and the learning rate (LR) schedule ( Tab. 12 ). Specifically, the LR schedule follows IR-SDE [ 52 ] , halving the LR every 200k steps. All other settings remain identical.

sections.heading: Ablation on Framework.
sections.text: Building upon the preceding optimization ablation, we strictly fix the EMA decay to 0.9999 and disable the LR schedule. Under this established baseline, we benchmark DiSI against representative degraded-to-clean interpolants: Standard SI [ 2 ] , IR-SDE [ 52 ] , and DDBM [ 106 ] . For fairness, all methods share the identical DULiT backbone and training protocol, differing solely in interpolants and corresponding samplers, with results in Tab. 5 .

sections.heading: Ablation on Regression Overhead.
sections.text: To isolate the extra architectural cost of DiSI-R compared to pure regression networks, we adopt the preceding optimization baseline with EMA decay fixed at 0.9999 and a constant LR of 1e-4 and remove the Conditional Branch and Time Embedding/Modulation modules in Tab. 14 . The w/o T&C variant is trained without noise perturbation to learn the deterministic LQ-to-GT mapping, mirroring an end-to-end regression network.

sections.heading: Ablation on Network Settings.
sections.text: Orthogonal to the progressive structural ablations below, we evaluate the prediction objective using the fully optimized baseline from Tab. 10 , predicting coupled velocities ( 𝒗 r , 𝒗 g ) (\bm{v}_{r},\bm{v}_{g}) instead of the target 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} in Tab. 7 . For subsequent component ablations, we initialize a baseline via an intermediate optimization setup (EMA decay 0.999, retaining the LR schedule).

sections.heading: Loss Weighting.
sections.text: Under the aforementioned specific baseline setup, we first ablate the dynamic adaptive loss weighting, with results summarized in Tab. 7 .

sections.heading: Long-Range Residual Connection.
sections.text: Enabling loss weighting, we proceed to ablate the long-range residual connection. We replace the standard additive connection (see Fig. 3 ) with a dynamic variant, scaling the noisy branch’s residual feature via a time-dependent weight linearly predicted from joint time embeddings in Sec. 0.F.1 . Additionally, we evaluate removing this connection entirely in Tab. 7 .

sections.heading: Time Modulation.
sections.text: Retaining the dynamic residual, we introduce single-branch modulation in Sec. 0.F.1 by removing time modulation from the degraded image branch, as the degraded input remains constant across time steps. Adopting the single-branch design, we integrate a level-shared adaptation of PixArt- α \alpha modulation [ 7 ] in Sec. 0.F.1 . While PixArt- α \alpha relies on a single global time projection with block-specific learnable offsets, DULiT’s varying channel dimensions prohibit this global approach. Consequently, we propose a level-shared approach: deploying one shared time projection per resolution level, where blocks within each level share base coefficients but maintain unique learnable offsets. Adopting the level-shared PixArt- α \alpha modulation, we systematically prune its parameters to reduce redundancy in Tab. 7 . The full mechanism (see Fig. 3 b) comprises pre-norm scales ζ ⋅ ⋅ \zeta_{\cdot}^{\cdot} , pre-norm shifts ε ⋅ ⋅ \varepsilon_{\cdot}^{\cdot} , and post-module scales ξ ⋅ ⋅ \xi_{\cdot}^{\cdot} , collectively denoted as ( ζ ⋅ ⋅ , ε ⋅ ⋅ , ξ ⋅ ⋅ ) (\zeta_{\cdot}^{\cdot},\varepsilon_{\cdot}^{\cdot},\xi_{\cdot}^{\cdot}) . We sequentially ablate the post-module scales ξ ⋅ ⋅ \xi_{\cdot}^{\cdot} (yielding the ( ζ ⋅ ⋅ , ε ⋅ ⋅ ) (\zeta_{\cdot}^{\cdot},\varepsilon_{\cdot}^{\cdot}) setting) and the pre-norm shifts ε ⋅ ⋅ \varepsilon_{\cdot}^{\cdot} (retaining only ζ ⋅ ⋅ \zeta_{\cdot}^{\cdot} ).

sections.heading: JLA Deisgn.
sections.text: Adopting the ( ζ ⋅ ⋅ , ε ⋅ ⋅ ) (\zeta_{\cdot}^{\cdot},\varepsilon_{\cdot}^{\cdot}) modulation, we first ablate the JLA module in Tab. 7 . We compare Linear and Conv projections, defining the latter as a pointwise 1 × 1 1\times 1 followed by a depthwise 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution. Additionally, we evaluate replacing the linear attention in DULiT’s middle block with standard attention ( i.e . , Vanilla ) implemented by flash-attention [ 15 ] .

sections.heading: FFN Design.
sections.text: Parallel to the JLA experiments, we independently ablate the FFN structure on the same ( ζ ⋅ ⋅ , ε ⋅ ⋅ ) (\zeta_{\cdot}^{\cdot},\varepsilon_{\cdot}^{\cdot}) baseline ( Tab. 7 ). Beyond comparing Linear and Conv projections, we investigate ConvGate , a convolutional adaptation of GeGLU [ 67 ] . While standard GeGLU splits linearly projected inputs channel-wise to multiply a GeLU-activated half with the other, our ConvGate replaces all linear projections with the aforementioned Conv layers.

sections.heading: Positional Embedding.
sections.text: Fixing both JLA and FFN to use Conv projections while retaining linear attention for JLA and the standard non-GeGLU structure for FFN, we evaluate applying RoPE [ 73 ] to the JLA mechanism in Sec. 0.F.1 .

sections.heading: Ablation on Time Samplers.
sections.text: To evaluate time samplers, we adopt a baseline incorporating all preceding architectural modification, specifically configuring Conv JLA and Linear FFN projections without positional embeddings. Using this fixed setup, we vary the training time samplers in Tabs. 8 and 15 .

sections.heading: Analysis of Inference Hyperparameters for Linear Trajectory.
sections.text: Ablating the Linear path ( Tab. 16 ) reveals: (1) Like the Elliptical path, generative capacity requires NFE > 2 \text{NFE}>2 , with η = 0 \eta=0 remaining optimal. (2) While enabling a regression-generation transition, the Linear path exhibits sharper fidelity drops under increased stochasticity than its Elliptical counterpart. (3) The regression baseline ( δ = 0 \delta=0 ) is inferior, likely due to the asymmetric sampling of r r around zero in the Linear Specialist Time Sampler ( Algorithm 2 ). Such asymmetry creates a less favorable condition for the model to learn a stable, deterministic regression mapping compared to the symmetric Elliptical case. These findings justify employing the Elliptical path for DiSI-G to maximize the fidelity-perception envelope.

Yichao Zhang E-mail {liuyi61,2432018,lwengen,jhguan,yichaozhang}@tongji.edu.cn, sgzhou@fudan.edu.cn Affiliation: Affiliation: Tongji University Abstract Recent advances in Image Restoration (IR) have been largely driven by generative methods such as Diffusion Models and Flow Matching, which excel in synthesizing realistic textures while suffering from slow multi-step inference and compromised pixel fidelity. In contrast, classical regression-based IR methods excel precisely in these aspects, offering single-step efficiency and high pixel-level reconstruction fidelity. To bridge this gap, we propose DiSI , a unified framework that Di sentangles the underlying S tochastic I nterpolant process into independent generation and regression components. This decoupling endows DiSI with remarkable versatility, enabling a continuous and controllable transition from a pure regression process to a fully generative one. Technically, we instantiate this framework with two specific sampling trajectories, accompanied by a unified sampler for high-quality, few-step inference on arbitrary trajectories. Furthermore, we design a dual-branch U-Net style transformer network in pixel space, using a dedicated branch to enhance conditional guidance while ensuring high throughput. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiSI efficiently achieves competitive results on various IR tasks, while uniquely offering the inference-time flexibility to control the distortion-perception trade-off within a single model. Keywords: Image Restoration Stochastic Interpolants Diffusion Models Disentanglement Figure 1 : (a-c) A conceptual comparison between our method DiSI and major existing generative frameworks DMs, FMs and SIs, illustrated by restoring a distorted 𝖲 \mathsf{S} curve. (a) DMs/FMs: a path between data 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} and noise 𝒛 \bm{z} . (b) SIs: a path between two data points ( 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} , 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} ) with intermediate noise. (c) DiSI : a decoupled framework with an independent Regression Time r r for the data-to-data path and a Generation Time g g for the noise component. Unlike (a-b) learning a single velocity 𝒗 θ \bm{v}_{\theta} , DiSI learns two decoupled velocities ( 𝒗 r θ , 𝒗 g θ \bm{v}^{\theta}_{r},\bm{v}^{\theta}_{g} ) for each time axis (see Sec. 3.2 ). (d) DiSI enables a smooth and controllable transition from one-step regression to multi-step generation by simply adjusting δ \delta (see Sec. 3.4 ), using the same trained model weights . 1 Introduction Image Restoration (IR) is a fundamental and long-standing problem in low-level vision that involves restoring high-quality images from their low-quality ( i.e . , degraded) counterparts [ 91 ] . It encompasses multiple tasks, including image super-resolution [ 38 , 81 , 65 , 103 , 102 ] , denoising [ 98 , 14 , 9 ] , and inpainting [ 58 , 39 , 50 ] . Solving these problems is essential for enhancing image quality and usability. Advances in deep learning have inspired a paradigm of regression-based IR methods, where networks [ 41 , 97 ] are trained to map degraded images to clean ones by minimizing a pixel-wise loss ( e.g . , MSE) [ 74 ] . Despite their efficiency and high performance on various distortion metrics ( e.g . , PSNR), they often yield over-smoothed or unrealistic textures, compromising perceptual quality [ 3 ] . To synthesize realistic textures, IR has embraced generative models, with Diffusion Models (DMs) [ 25 , 71 , 72 ] and Flow Matching (FM) [ 46 , 42 ] now dominating this field. DMs and FMs involve a forward process adding noise, and a backward process reconstructing samples from Gaussian noise (see Fig. 1 a), conditioned on degraded images [ 11 , 65 ] . However, this is unnecessary and inefficient for IR, as the degraded image itself offers a better starting point than pure noise. This insight inspires recent works, e.g . , residual diffusion models [ 94 , 45 ] , Mean-Reverting Diffusion Models (MRDMs) [ 52 , 53 ] , and Diffusion Bridges (DBs) [ 106 , 44 , 93 ] , to construct a direct degraded-to-clean diffusion path. A unifying framework is provided by Stochastic Interpolants (SIs) [ 1 , 55 ] that generalize DMs/FMs by defining transitions between arbitrary distributions. This naturally supports direct degraded-to-clean paths (see Fig. 1 b), particularly suitable for IR [ 2 ] . Despite their powerful ability to synthesize realistic textures, DM/FM-based generative IR methods introduce a critical trade-off. They require expensive multi-step inference and often sacrifice the pixel-level fidelity in exchange for their remarkable perceptual quality [ 52 , 44 , 2 ] . In contrast, high-fidelity restoration and single-step efficiency are precisely where the regression paradigm [ 97 , 41 ] excels. This fundamental dichotomy between distortion and perception [ 3 ] , separating regressive methods that prioritize fidelity and efficiency from generative methods that achieve perceptual quality at a high cost, motivates the following question: Can we develop a unified framework to seamlessly bridge regression and generation, thereby enabling fine-grained control over both aspects? To answer this question, this paper presents DiSI , a new framework that Di sentangles generation and regression within S tochastic I nterpolants ( Fig. 1 c). In standard SIs ( Fig. 1 b) [ 2 , 1 ] , the generative capability stems from the stochastic noise term γ t ​ 𝒛 \gamma_{t}\bm{z} , while the deterministic path between 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} and 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} inherently constitutes a regression. DiSI decouples these by introducing two independent time variables: Regression Time r r governing the deterministic transition, and Generation Time g g controlling noise injection. This explicit separation directly bridges regression and generation, enabling fine-grained control over the fundamental distortion-perception trade-off. As shown in Fig. 1 d, DiSI can seamlessly transition from a one-step, high-fidelity regression that over-smooths textures, to a multi-step generation process capable of synthesizing rich, realistic details. In the DiSI framework, we design two specific sampling trajectories: an elliptical trajectory analogous to DBs [ 44 , 106 , 93 ] and a linear trajectory inspired by MRDMs [ 52 , 53 ] . We also introduce a unified efficient first-order sampler, enabling high-quality, few-step restoration on arbitrary trajectories. To further improve performance and efficiency, we propose a novel dual-branch U-Net style transformer (DULiT) in pixel space, inspired by [ 17 , 88 , 97 ] . It strengthens conditional guidance from degraded images via its dual-branch design, while incorporating efficient modules like linear attention [ 33 ] to ensure high throughput. Our technical contributions are: 1) DiSI, a novel framework that decouples regression and generation within SI for controllable distortion-perception balance. 2) Two sampling trajectories accompanied by an efficient and analytically derived sampler for fast, high-quality inference. 3) A dual-branch pixel-space network that strengthens conditional guidance while maintaining high efficiency. 2 Related Work Image Restoration. IR is a long-standing and fundamental problem in low-level vision, with tasks such as image deraining [ 90 ] , deblurring [ 100 ] , and super-resolution [ 82 ] . Deep learning has established neural networks as the prevailing IR approach, commonly implemented via convolutional architectures [ 103 , 102 , 4 , 98 ] or vision transformers [ 97 , 60 , 41 , 6 ] , and trained with regression losses. While these methods achieve strong distortion metrics like PSNR and SSIM [ 83 ] , they often yield unrealistic outputs in highly ill-posed scenarios like inpainting [ 87 , 50 ] . The advancement of IR has been significantly driven by generative models [ 22 , 25 ] , with DMs and FMs now dominating the field [ 40 , 23 ] . Most DM/FM-based IR methods start from pure noise and condition on degraded images [ 50 , 86 , 80 , 64 , 65 , 10 ] . Others, more aligned with our work, modify the initial distribution to incorporate degraded inputs, including MRDMs [ 52 , 53 ] , Diffusion Bridges (DBs) [ 93 , 44 , 106 , 104 ] , and SI models [ 2 ] . While generative IR methods excel at producing realistic textures, they may compromise pixel-level fidelity. Diffusion Models. DMs [ 12 ] are a prominent class of probabilistic generative models [ 76 ] for image synthesis [ 16 ] , pioneered by DDPM [ 25 ] and NCSN [ 71 ] . Since their introduction, the theoretical scope of DMs has been significantly extended by Score Matching [ 72 , 31 ] and, more recently Flow Matching (FM) [ 42 , 46 ] with the concept of differential equations. The latter have already become foundational to image generation [ 17 , 62 ] . A broader perspective is offered by Stochastic Interpolant (SI) [ 1 , 55 ] , a generalized framework bridging arbitrary distributions that unifies DMs and FMs, providing our theoretical basis. The rapid evolution of DMs and FMs has catalyzed significant advancements, with innovations in network architecture and sampling efficiency being particularly relevant to this work. Architecturally, backbones have transitioned from standard U-Nets [ 57 , 16 ] to scalable Transformers [ 79 ] ( e.g . , DiT [ 59 ] and MM-DiT [ 17 ] ), with recent research increasingly prioritizing efficiency [ 88 , 13 , 7 ] . Concurrently, substantial efforts have focused on accelerating the iterative inference process [ 18 , 70 , 46 , 21 , 48 , 47 ] , where advanced solvers like DDIM [ 69 ] and DPM-Solver [ 48 , 49 , 105 ] reduce sampling steps while maintaining generation quality. 3 Method 3.1 Preliminary As introduced in [ 2 , 1 ] , the stochastic interpolant (SI) process is defined as 1 1 1 The general SI form [ 1 ] is defined as 𝒙 t = 𝑰 ⁡ ( t , 𝒙 0 , 𝒙 1 ) + γ t ​ 𝒛 \bm{x}_{t}=\bm{I}(t,\bm{x}_{0},\bm{x}_{1})+\gamma_{t}\bm{z} , subject to 𝑰 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝒙 0 , 𝒙 1 ) = 𝒙 0 \bm{I}(0,\bm{x}_{0},\bm{x}_{1})=\bm{x}_{0} and 𝑰 ⁡ ( 1 , 𝒙 0 , 𝒙 1 ) = 𝒙 1 \bm{I}(1,\bm{x}_{0},\bm{x}_{1})=\bm{x}_{1} . We adopt the SI framework because it unifies these models and fits IR’s data-to-data nature [ 2 ] . However, standard SIs have a critical limitation: they fuse the deterministic regression path with the stochastic generative process by coupling both to a single time variable t t . Hence, our core insight is that fine-grained control over the regression-generation balance requires disentangling these processes. Motivated by this insight, we reformulate the standard SI process in Eq. 1 by introducing two independent time variables ( Fig. 1 c): 1) a Regression Time r r governing the data-to-data transition ( i.e . , 𝒙 1 → 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{1}\to\bm{x}_{0} ), and 2) a Generation Time g g controlling the injected noise 𝒛 \bm{z} . This formulation explicitly disentangles the regression path α r ​ 𝒙 0 + β r ​ 𝒙 1 \alpha_{r}\bm{x}_{0}+\beta_{r}\bm{x}_{1} from the noise injection, overcoming the single-variable constraint of standard SIs and enabling independent control of the two processes. We adopt a dual-branch structure from MM-DiT [ 17 ] to enhance conditional guidance, processing the noisy state 𝒙 ⁡ ( r , g ) \bm{x}\left(r,g\right) and the degraded image 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} in parallel. However, the constant-resolution pipeline of DiT backbones [ 59 , 17 ] is computationally expensive. To address this, we integrate the dual-branch design into a hierarchical U-Net backbone, motivated by [ 63 , 13 , 97 ] . As shown in Fig. 3 , the DULiT backbone features a three-stage encoder with L 1 L_{1} , L 2 L_{2} , L 3 L_{3} DULiT blocks, a middle layer with L 4 L_{4} blocks, and a symmetric decoder. The encoder downsamples features via PixelUnshuffle [ 68 ] and 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution, while the decoder upsamples using 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution and PixelShuffle [ 68 ] . Dual-Branch Skip Connections are applied per branch at each resolution level. Inspired by HDiT [ 13 ] , we use an efficient learnable linear interpolation (lerp) for image fusions. Input and output features are processed with 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolutions, augmented by a long-range residual connection that improves performance. To accelerate convergence, following [ 31 , 32 ] , we zero-initialize all DULiT output projections and replace biases with a channel of ones concatenated to the input. B. DULiT Block. The core computational unit for all stages is our DULiT Block (see Fig. 3 (b)). We use AdaGroupNorm [ 16 ] for time conditioning, which, unlike AdaLayerNorm used in DiT [ 59 ] , avoids costly reshape operations. Within each block, the Joint Linear Attention (JLA) layer is the only cross-branch interaction module, followed by FeedForward Networks (FFNs) for both branches. C. JLA Layer. The Joint Linear Attention (JLA) layer forms the core of our DULiT Block. To address the prohibitive quadratic complexity of vanilla attention [ 79 , 59 ] in high-resolution pixel space, following Sana [ 88 ] , we employ ReLU linear attention [ 33 ] ( Fig. 3 (c)) that eliminates the softmax operator and reorders matrix operations for linear computational complexity. Our key innovation lies in its joint design ( Fig. 3 (d)): features from both noisy and conditional branches pass through efficient Projection blocks, which are composed of 1 × 1 1\times 1 Conv and 3 × 3 3\times 3 DWConv layers inspired by [ 26 , 97 ] , to generate dual-branch 𝑸 \bm{Q} , 𝑲 \bm{K} , and 𝑽 \bm{V} . These tensors are concatenated along the sequence dimension, a strategy empirically superior to channel-wise fusion as validated in Tab. 7 . To ensure efficiency, we accelerate the entire JLA layer using torch.compile . D. FFN. The DULiT Block concludes with an efficient FFN ( Fig. 3 (e)). It replaces the FFN in MM-DiT [ 17 ] with a computationally efficient design, using the same Projection block as in the JLA layer, and a GELU activation. E. Time Embedding and Modulation. Time variables ( r , g ) (r,g) are individually encoded and summed into a token t t ( Fig. 3 (a)). As in DiT [ 59 ] , t t is projected per block to generate scale/shift parameters for both branches, modulating normalized features before JLA and FFN ( Fig. 3 (b)). To demonstrate flexible trade-offs between regression and generation, we present two variants: (1) DiSI-R for fidelity via noiseless ( δ = 0 \delta=0 , i.e . , regression) sampling, and (2) DiSI-G for perceptual quality via noisy ( δ > 0 \delta>0 ) sampling. Both share the same trained weights and only differ in sampling parameters (see Sec. 0.D.1 ). Based on the results, we observe: (1) DM/FM-based baselines excel in perceptual metrics ( e.g . , LPIPS, FID) but lag in distortion metrics ( e.g . , PSNR, SSIM), and their multi-step inference incurs significant computational overhead. (2) DiSI generally achieves competitive or even SOTA performance across the four tasks, demonstrating strong restoration capability. (3) DiSI-R excels in distortion metrics with high efficiency, while DiSI-G achieves remarkable perceptual quality at increased computational cost. Visually, DiSI-R often yields over-smoothed results, whereas DiSI-G produces realistic textures (see Fig. 7 ). Crucially, this transition requires no retraining and is achieved solely by tuning sampling parameters ( e.g . , δ \delta and sampling steps), enabling a controllable distortion-perception performance balance within a single trained model. (4) DiSI outperforms DM/FM-based baselines in efficiency while maintaining competitive generative performance, owing to our DULiT network and few-step sampler. 4.2 Ablation Studies All ablation experiments are conducted on the Rain100H dataset. We additionally report the Number of Function Evaluations (NFE) to assess inference efficiency. For more detailed settings of ablation experiments, see Sec. 0.D.4 . A. Effect of Framework. To validate our framework, we benchmark DiSI against representative degraded-to-clean interpolant methods, including Standard SI [ 2 ] , MRDMs ( e.g . , IR-SDE [ 52 ] ), and DBs ( e.g . , DDBM [ 106 ] ). For fairness, all methods employ the same DULiT backbone and training protocol, differing only in their interpolant definitions and corresponding samplers. As shown in Tab. 5 , DiSI significantly outperforms previous baselines, such as IR-SDE and DDBM, across all metrics under the same network capacity. Notably, Standard SI achieves performance comparable to our generative mode (DiSI-G), which is theoretically expected as SI functions as a static special case of DiSI (see Fig. 1 ). However, unlike SI, DiSI offers inference-time controllability: DiSI-R yields the best distortion metrics and efficiency, while DiSI-G optimizes perceptual quality, unifying regression and generation under a single framework.
